    Trajectory inference with Palantir and PAGA¶

    Python port of the R vignette Trajectory inference with Palantir and PAGA. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

    Intro¶

    Two trajectory methods live in bixverse, both operating on the kNN graph you already built with bv.graph.find_neighbours().

    Palantir (Setty et al., 2019) models differentiation as a Markov chain over a multiscale diffusion map of the cells. Out come a pseudotime per cell, the probability of each cell reaching each terminal state, and the differentiation entropy derived from those probabilities. It needs a start cell and, optionally, the terminal states.

    PAGA (Wolf et al., 2019) abstracts the cell-level graph into a cluster-level one, where the edge weight between two clusters measures how much more connected they are than a random null model expects. Its maximum spanning forest is the backbone people usually draw. PAGA needs a clustering and nothing else.

    The data set is the one from the Palantir sample notebook: 4142 human CD34+ bone marrow cells across 16106 genes, already filtered. Three lineages come out of it, erythroid, monocyte and dendritic cell, all seeded from a haematopoietic stem cell pool.

    The two supporting pieces from that notebook are here too. MAGIC (van Dijk et al., 2018) smooths counts over the same kNN graph, which is what makes the marker plots readable. Gene trends fit a landmark Gaussian process per branch, the Mellon-based estimator the reference uses rather than the legacy GAM. Both are restricted to a gene subset in bixverse, for reasons spelled out where they come up.

    Feature selection, PCA and neighbours¶

    Standard pipeline. The one choice worth spelling out is k = 30 on the kNN graph: Palantir builds its diffusion kernel from whatever graph is stored on the object, and 30 neighbours is what the reference uses. The distance metric has to be euclidean, since the diffusion kernel is a Gaussian over a metric distance and cosine is not one.

    pruning does not have to move with k. A Jaccard threshold p asks two cells to share a fraction 2p / (1 + p) of their neighbourhoods, whatever k is, so the default 1/16 keeps the same ~12% at k = 30 as at k = 15.

    MAGIC imputation¶

    MAGIC builds a row-stochastic operator over the kNN graph and applies it three times, so every cell becomes a weighted average of its neighbourhood. It is the same adaptive-bandwidth kernel Palantir uses for its diffusion map, so the two agree on what a neighbourhood is.

    bv.pp.run_magic() writes the result onto the object as a cached layer, sc.cache.magic. It takes a gene list rather than doing everything, and that is deliberate: the output is dense, and the whole point of the on-disk store is not holding a dense cells-by-genes matrix. Pick the genes you want to look at.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    bv.pp.run_magic(sc, markers)

magic = sc.cache.magic
assert magic is not None

print(f"{magic.data.shape[0]} cells x {magic.data.shape[1]} genes: {magic.features}")
    bv.pp.run_magic(sc, markers) magic = sc.cache.magic assert magic is not None print(f"{magic.data.shape[0]} cells x {magic.data.shape[1]} genes: {magic.features}")
    Running MAGIC over the rna kNN graph (4142 cells, 4 genes, 3 steps).

    MAGIC: imputed 4 genes across 4142 cells in 757.50µs
4142 cells x 4 genes: ['CD34' 'MPO' 'GATA1' 'IRF8']

    Every extractor takes layer="magic", and feature_plot() passes it straight through.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    bv.pl.feature_plot(sc, markers, "umap", palette="spectral", layer="magic")
plt.show()
    bv.pl.feature_plot(sc, markers, "umap", palette="spectral", layer="magic") plt.show()

    That is the picture people know from the paper, and it is worth being clear about what produced it. Neighbourhoods overlap, so smoothing over them makes nearby cells resemble each other in every gene at once. Gene-gene correlation after imputation is inflated, badly, and the inflation is a property of the graph rather than of the biology. Do not feed these values into Hotspot, SCENIC, differential correlation or CoReMo: those methods measure exactly the quantity MAGIC manufactures, and they will report the graph back to you as a finding. extract_dot_plot_data() has no layer argument for the same reason.

    The layer is tracked like every other cached artefact, so it goes stale when the graph under it moves.

    PAGA¶

    PAGA is the cheap one, so start there. It reads the kNN indices and a clustering, ignores the distances entirely, and gives back a clusters-by-clusters graph.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    paga_res = bv.traj.run_paga(sc, "leiden_clusters")
assert paga_res is not None

paga_res

    paga_plot() puts every cluster at the centroid of its cells in an embedding and draws the graph over them. A free layout of the abstracted graph would put the nodes somewhere arbitrary, which you then have to relate back to the UMAP by eye.

plt.show()

    Edge thresholding is not optional. The abstracted graph is close to complete on real data, so at threshold=0 you get a hairball. tree_only=True is the shortcut to the backbone, and it is the readable one on anything above a handful of clusters.

    Palantir¶

    The start cell and the three terminal states come straight from the reference notebook. The start cell was picked there for high CD34 expression; the terminal states are one cell each in the dendritic, monocyte and erythroid tips.

    In [16]:
    Copied! 
    early_cell = "Run5_164698952452459"

terminal_states = {
    "DC": "Run5_131097901611291",
    "Mono": "Run5_134936662236454",
    "Ery": "Run4_200562869397916",
}
    early_cell = "Run5_164698952452459" terminal_states = { "DC": "Run5_131097901611291", "Mono": "Run5_134936662236454", "Ery": "Run4_200562869397916", }

    knn=30 is the neighbour count for the geodesic graph Palantir builds on the multiscale space, a different knob from the k of the input kNN graph. num_waypoints stays at its 1200 default; the reference notebook drops it to 500.

    Two things do not mirror the reference, and both change what you get.

    use_early_cell_as_start is True, so the early cell you name is the one that gets used. The reference snaps it to the nearest boundary cell of the diffusion map instead, and that candidate set is small, at most two cells per multiscale component. On a branching manifold the snap will cheerfully move a root cell onto a branch tip and run the whole trajectory backwards.

    n_eigs is pinned at 10, leaving nine multiscale components. Left at None the count comes from the largest eigengap, and nothing stops that from landing on 3, i.e. two components. Two components cannot resolve a three-way branch: the erythroid arm separates fine but the monocyte and dendritic fate probabilities end up correlated, their branch masks collapse onto each other, and the gene trends for those two lineages come out nearly identical. There is a section on that below.

    In [17]:
    Copied! 
    palantir_res = bv.traj.run_palantir(
    sc,
    early_cell,
    terminal_states=terminal_states,
    palantir_params=PalantirParams(n_eigs=10, knn=30),
    seed=42,
)
assert palantir_res is not None

palantir_res
    palantir_res = bv.traj.run_palantir( sc, early_cell, terminal_states=terminal_states, palantir_params=PalantirParams(n_eigs=10, knn=30), seed=42, ) assert palantir_res is not None palantir_res

    PalantirRes(
  n_cells=4142,
  n_terminal_states=3,
  modality='rna',

    Two things to watch in that print out. Repair edges above zero means the kNN graph was disconnected and had to be bridged, which usually means k is too small for the data. A note about the diffusion eigensolve not converging means the embedding is under-resolved, and every distance taken on it is suspect; raise lanczos_max_restarts in PalantirParams before believing anything downstream.

    Results back onto the object¶

    PalantirRes is keyed by cell id, not position, so join it onto obs on cell_id rather than assuming the two are in the same order.

    In [18]:
    Copied! 
    obs_cells = sc.obs(cols=["cell_idx", "cell_id"], filtered=True)

sc.add_obs(
    obs_cells.join(palantir_res.pseudotime, on="cell_id", how="left").select(
        "cell_idx",
        pl.col("pseudotime").alias("palantir_pseudotime"),
        pl.col("entropy").alias("palantir_entropy"),
    )
)
    obs_cells = sc.obs(cols=["cell_idx", "cell_id"], filtered=True) sc.add_obs( obs_cells.join(palantir_res.pseudotime, on="cell_id", how="left").select( "cell_idx", pl.col("pseudotime").alias("palantir_pseudotime"), pl.col("entropy").alias("palantir_entropy"), ) )

    The fate probability frame has one column per terminal state. Because terminal_states was a dict, its keys are already the column names, so all that is left is the dominant fate per cell.

    In [19]:
    Copied! 
    lineages = palantir_res.branches

fate_probs = obs_cells.join(palantir_res.branch_probs, on="cell_id", how="left")

prob_mat = fate_probs.select(lineages).to_numpy()

sc.add_obs(
    fate_probs.select(
        "cell_idx",
        *[pl.col(lineage).alias(f"fate_{lineage}") for lineage in lineages],
    ).with_columns(
        pl.Series(
            "palantir_branch", np.asarray(lineages)[prob_mat.argmax(axis=1)]
        ).cast(pl.Enum(lineages))
    )
)

fate_probs.select("cell_id", pl.col(lineages).round(3)).head()
    lineages = palantir_res.branches fate_probs = obs_cells.join(palantir_res.branch_probs, on="cell_id", how="left") prob_mat = fate_probs.select(lineages).to_numpy() sc.add_obs( fate_probs.select( "cell_idx", *[pl.col(lineage).alias(f"fate_{lineage}") for lineage in lineages], ).with_columns( pl.Series( "palantir_branch", np.asarray(lineages)[prob_mat.argmax(axis=1)] ).cast(pl.Enum(lineages)) ) ) fate_probs.select("cell_id", pl.col(lineages).round(3)).head()

    Rows do not necessarily sum to one. Fate probabilities below branch_prob_threshold (0.01 by default) are zeroed without renormalisation, and cells whose waypoint weight sits on a stranded waypoint lose that mass entirely.

    Pseudotime and entropy¶

    In [20]:
    Copied! 
    bv.pl.embedding_plot(
    sc,
    "umap",
    "palantir_pseudotime",
    palette="spectral",
    discrete=False,
)
plt.show()
    bv.pl.embedding_plot( sc, "umap", "palantir_pseudotime", palette="spectral", discrete=False, ) plt.show()

    The same quantity on the abstracted graph is worth a look, because it is the cheapest check that the two methods agree. PAGA knows nothing about pseudotime, so if its backbone and the pseudotime gradient point in different directions, one of them is wrong.

    In [21]:
    Copied! 
    bv.pl.paga_plot(
    sc,
    paga_res,
    embedding="umap",
    node_colour_by="palantir_pseudotime",
    palette="spectral",
    tree_only=True,
)
plt.show()
    bv.pl.paga_plot( sc, paga_res, embedding="umap", node_colour_by="palantir_pseudotime", palette="spectral", tree_only=True, ) plt.show()

    Entropy is high where a cell still has several fates open to it and drops to zero once it commits. Three equally likely fates give log(3), the ceiling. Here the stem pool sits below it, because the monocyte fate already carries more than its third of the probability there.

    In [22]:
    Copied! 
    print(
    f"max entropy {palantir_res.pseudotime['entropy'].max():.3f}, "
    f"log(3) = {np.log(3):.3f}"
)

    Letting Palantir find the terminal states¶

    Drop terminal_states and they get detected from the waypoint Markov chain instead. Handy when you have no prior, but treat the result as a starting point rather than an answer: the detection reads extremes of the multiscale space, and on data sets this size those are not always well determined.

    Gene trends¶

    bv.traj.run_gene_trends() does two things. First it assigns cells to branches: for each fate, the probability threshold is an expanding quantile over the pseudotime-sorted cells, made monotone with a cumulative maximum, so a fate's bar can only rise as differentiation proceeds. Then it fits a landmark Gaussian process with a Matern-5/2 kernel per branch, on a 500 point pseudotime grid.

    CD34 peaks early on the DC and monocyte arms and then falls on all three, GATA1 climbs on the erythroid arm, MPO on the monocyte one, IRF8 on the dendritic one. Set use_magic=True to fit the imputed layer instead, which is what the reference notebook does. Note that the GP already smooths over pseudotime, so imputing first smooths twice.

    branch_cells carries the selection itself, which is the branch cell set the reference notebook plots.

    The same trick works with any per-cell quantity. A smoothed curve through the entropy column watches commitment happen along the trajectory. There is no loess in numpy, so a running median over the pseudotime-sorted cells of each dominant fate stands in for it.

    Where this can go wrong¶

    Palantir has more moving parts than most methods in this package, and several of them fail quietly rather than loudly. In rough order of how often they bite:

    • Pruning too hard. Upstream of Palantir entirely. It costs you clusters, not pseudotime, but a one-cell cluster then walks into PAGA and comes back out as a fat edge into a dot, because the null model has almost no possible edges to normalise against. rescue=True (the default) reconnects the small components pruning cuts off, so this mainly bites with it switched off.
    • The start cell. Covered above. Set use_early_cell_as_start=False to get the reference behaviour and it can move your root onto a branch tip. If pseudotime comes back anti-correlated with what you expect, check start_cell on the result object first. Note that pseudotime is not pinned to zero at the start cell either: the refinement can put the minimum on a neighbour, and a start cell far from zero means it disagreed with your anchor.
    • eigen_converged is False. The diffusion eigensolve ran out of restarts, so the multiscale embedding is under-resolved. Everything downstream converges happily on noise, which is exactly why this is reported in run_info. Raise lanczos_max_restarts.
    • repair_edges > 0. The kNN graph was disconnected and Palantir bridged it to carry on. Raise k on find_neighbours() rather than living with the bridges.
    • stranded_waypoints > 0. Waypoints from which no terminal state is reachable. Their cells lose fate probability mass, so rows sum below one. A large count means the pseudotime-directed pruning cut too hard.
    • n_eigs. The one that bites hardest, and it is silent. Left at None the eigenvector count comes from the largest eigengap, and if that lands on 3 it leaves two multiscale components for a three-way branch. Nothing errors. What happens instead is that two of the three fates stop separating: their probabilities correlate, the branch selection hands the two branches almost the same cells, and their gene trends come out on top of each other. If two lineages give you the same curve, count the components before you blame the estimator. The check is below.
    • Branch masks are permissive by design. Even at a sensible n_eigs, a cell belongs to a branch when its fate probability is near the top of what has been seen up to its pseudotime, so the uncommitted trunk sits in every branch at once. That is the reference's logic and it is the right one, but it means two branches only diverge where their late cells differ. Check branch_cells overlap before reading much into two curves that hug.
    • The gene trend defaults are prior-dominated. Pseudotime is min-max scaled to [0, 1], so the reference's length_scale = 1 spans the entire domain and its sigma = 1 sits at roughly the signal scale of log-normalised expression. Almost any gene resolves into a smooth monotone or single-peaked curve. That is a presentation choice, not inference. Shorten length_scale in GeneTrendsParams before believing a bump.
    • Double smoothing. MAGIC averages over the graph and the GP averages over pseudotime. Running both is defensible for a figure and rarely necessary for the trend itself. If a feature only shows up with use_magic=True, that is worth knowing about.
    • A stale imputed layer. The layer is stamped against the kNN graph it came from, so sc.cache_status() flags it once the graph or the cell filter moves. run_gene_trends(use_magic=True) refuses to fit a stale one.

    Counting the components: the multiscale frame has one column per component. The run below leaves n_eigs at the eigengap default and compares the monocyte and dendritic branch masks against the pinned run.

    In [32]:
    Copied! 
    palantir_gap = bv.traj.run_palantir(
    sc,
    early_cell,
    terminal_states=terminal_states,
    palantir_params=PalantirParams(knn=30),
    seed=42,
)
assert palantir_gap is not None

rows = []
for label, res in [("eigengap", palantir_gap), ("n_eigs = 10", palantir_res)]:
    branch_cells = bv.traj.run_gene_trends(sc, res, features=["CD34"]).branch_cells
    mono, dc = set(branch_cells["Mono"]), set(branch_cells["DC"])
    rows.append(
        {
            "n_eigs": label,
            "components": res.multiscale.width - 1,
            "mono_cells": len(mono),
            "dc_cells": len(dc),
            "shared": len(mono & dc),
            "mono_only": len(mono - dc),
        }
    )

pl.DataFrame(rows)

    On this run the eigengap keeps five components, enough for the three fates to separate, and the overlap barely moves against the pinned run. The eigengap hangs off the kNN graph though, so it moves with k, the HVGs and the PCA. Pinning n_eigs takes it out of the equation.
